doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Taking a drum solo and being musical
summary: Roker sings the melody when soloing, wants dynamics and pulse, and says drummers were mostly accompanists for dancers; Woods tells of a Ramsey Lewis drummer going soft.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You know I wanted to ask you about taking a drum solo. You know a lot of people don’t really know how to listen to a drum solo. Many times when a drummer takes a solo on the form, the audience isn’t even counting anymore. They’re not even staying with him. Talk to us about the whole art of taking a solo on a percussion instrument.

Well the way I solo I keep the melody in mind. I always sing the melody. See drummers make great singers because they don’t get changes to play, so they’ve got to keep the melody in mind. And if you do that, you can put, the rhythm is so infinite man that there’s so much you can do. But when people listen to a drummer play they want energy man, they want dynamics, they want the same thing that the drummer wants. It’s up to the guy taking the solo to sell himself to the people that’s listening you know. It’s up to the player to make the people want to listen to him. So whatever, soloing is a different art. Some people can just solo man. Some people are natural soloists. Some people have to really work hard to really play an interesting solo. You know, and be clever, and still be basic.

You know I had a chance, I was playing in a orchestra. I was playing the string bass in the string section behind Ramsey Lewis one night. And his drummer was basically saying he realized he was not a power drummer. So he got his excitement, he played a chorus and about every eight measures he got softer and softer and softer. He said “no I’m not going to overpower this drumset. I’m going to do it just exact opposite way. I’m going to give you things you don’t expect. You don’t expect the drums to be soft.” So he started
out pretty good, and then every eight measures he got softer. He went down to brushes. Finally he put the brushes down and said “Just beat on the chest.”

Well he was some showman. You need some of that too. But soloing is a different art form. Because drummers, when I come up, we were mostly accompanists. You know we might not get a solo all night. Because most of the bands played dance music. And you know you can tell if a drummer has good time, if he gets a solo and he’s playing dance music if the people still dance, then he’s playing with feeling and he’s playing with pulse. You’ve got to have pulse, you’ve got to have feeling, you’ve got to have dynamics, there’s so much you’ve got to think of just to get from one note to the other one. It’s not all technique and you know energy. I mean some drummers play a solo and they’re just playing a lot of energy you know? And there’s no music, they forget about the music. So I think that a drummer should also be musical. Because then it’s easier to listen to. And then everybody that you’re playing with, they know where you’re at. You know they know where you’re at in the song in terms of the song. Because you’ve got to play the song too.
